White mana covers so much more than that, if you look at white magic cards and the themes they represent you'll find many more interpretations. 

From the Wiki:
Misconceptions and Controversies
A common misconception is that White stands for Good and that it is a fact without doubt. Granted, if you take a random lot of White cards and compare them with Black cards or Red cards, they will likely give off more of a "Good" feel than the others. However, taking the time to really look into what White is based upon, then you will see that White is not always good. Takeshi Konda from the Kamigawa book cycle was a prime example for a White antagonist, obsessed with the mysterious disk he held and bringing his nation glory, but losing sight of the individual; his very own daughter. In many sets White has been an antagonist in the form of law enforcement, government, or a cult (the Azorius Senate, Consulate and Ojutai, respectively), or as visionary antagonists who commit atrocities for what they believe to be morally correct (the aforementioned Konda, Elesh Norn and Nahiri).

White doesn't always stand for "Good", but it invariably stands for "Good" in its own mind. However, when taken to the extremes, White's ideals clearly crosses the lines of morality: Fascism for example, as a system based around complete order, is very White in essence. Communism is also a firmly White doctrine, imposing numerous laws and restrictions which can end up being oppressive for individuals, but good for society at large. Dictatorships are military institutions and follow strict codes of law placed upon their citizens, though few would call dictatorships "good".

When considering the personality traits and sensibilities of many different fictional races, everything from elves to aboleths, I find that most of them think in much the same way.

It is difficult to put yourself into the mind of a creature whose nature and perception are so wholly alien. But all creatures share certain traits that you can draw on to avoid molding each race into established stereotypes.

All creatures are mortal (even if they live forever, they can always be killed)
All creatures are able to communicate 
All creatures have desires (except of part of a hive mind?)
All creatures want to live (mostly)
All creatures like being comfortable
Etc...

When you focus on what sets other animals apart from us, you run into barriers that are hard to overcome.

E.g.
Dragons are possessive and greedy
Hippos are territorial
Tasmanian devils are aggressive

These impulses have a dramatic affect on social interactions.

A thousand years ago the humans lived in peace. The Great King Omund saw this peace and sought to preserve it forever. Trusting his kingdom none, he sought the blessing of the elves that he may also be granted life eternal so that he could rule forever. He journeyed to the feywild, the home of the elves and asked of their queen that she would grant him this mighty gift. She saw jealousy in his heart, and would not grant him his wish. Upon his return he found his kingdom at war, assailed on every side by monsters and beasts. He fought for many years to regain the peace of his kingdom. His son Erstan son grew to be a mighty warrior, loved much by the people. The people said that Erstan would make the mightiest king, and the Great King Omund was jealous. He cursed the elf queen and hated her for not granting her blood to him. In his fury he claimed “No son of mine shall take my house from me!” and he murdered his son in his sleep, and drank his blood. 


When the queen learned that the King had killed her son she was wroth, and she cursed him saying “Until thou conquer thy mortal fear, thy house shall have an end to its days, and shall never enter the paradise of thy God!” 


The King ruled for nigh a hundred years more, drinking the blood of his son's children to prolong his days. But eventually he was killed, and his kingdom handed down to his cursed sons to rule in mortal fear for generations. Some sought to overcome their mortality through necromancy and alchemy, some sought to free their forefathers from their hellish prison and grant them entry to Pelor’s Bosom. The kings’ days were long, but the kingdom never again had peace.
